claim: Upon antigen stimulation, T lymphocytes undergo dramatic changes in metabolism to fulfill the bioenergetic, biosynthetic and redox demands of proliferation and differentiation.
source: Upon antigen stimulation, T lymphocytes undergo dramatic changes in metabolism to fulfill the bioenergetic, biosynthetic and redox demands of proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is a general statement about T cell metabolism that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Glutathione (GSH) plays an essential role in controlling redox balance and cell fate.
source: Glutathione (GSH) plays an essential role in controlling redox balance and cell fate.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The inhibition of GSH recycling from GSSG does not impact GSH content and murine T cell fate.
source: While GSH can be recycled from Glutathione disulfide (GSSG), the inhibition of this recycling pathway does not impact GSH content and murine T cell fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Gsr knockout mice showing comparable GSH levels and T cell differentiation to wild-type.

claim: The inhibition of de novo synthesis of GSH by deleting Gclc dampens intracellular GSH, increases ROS, and impacts T cell differentiation.
source: By contrast, the inhibition of the de novo synthesis of GSH, by deleting either the catalytic (Gclc) or the modifier (Gclm) subunit of glutamate–cysteine ligase (Gcl), dampens intracellular GSH, increases ROS, and impact T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Gclc knockout mice showing reduced GSH, increased ROS, and altered T cell differentiation.

claim: The inhibition of de novo synthesis of GSH by deleting Gclm dampens intracellular GSH, increases ROS, and impacts T cell differentiation.
source: By contrast, the inhibition of the de novo synthesis of GSH, by deleting either the catalytic (Gclc) or the modifier (Gclm) subunit of glutamate–cysteine ligase (Gcl), dampens intracellular GSH, increases ROS, and impact T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Gclm knockout mice showing reduced GSH, increased ROS, and altered T cell differentiation.

claim: The inhibition of GSH de novo synthesis dampened the pathological progression of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
source: Moreover, the inhibition of GSH de novo synthesis dampened the pathological progression of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
evidence: This is supported by EAE experiments in Gclm and Gclc knockout mice showing reduced disease progression.

claim: Glutamine provides essential precursors for GSH biosynthesis.
source: We further reveal that glutamine provides essential precursors for GSH biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing experiments showing glutamine-derived glutamate incorporation into GSH.

claim: Glutamine catabolism fuels de novo synthesis of GSH and directs the lineage choice in T cells.
source: Our findings suggest that glutamine catabolism fuels de novo synthesis of GSH and directs the lineage choice in T cells.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experiments showing glutamine's role in GSH synthesis and T cell differentiation.

claim: GSH is the most abundant antioxidant capable of providing reducing equivalents.
source: Glutathione (GSH) is the most abundant antioxidant capable of providing reducing equivalents and it also serves as a versatile nucleophilic cofactor in a wide spectrum of metabolic reactions in aerobic organisms (Kosower and Kosower, 1978; Meister, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GSH serves as a versatile nucleophilic cofactor in a wide spectrum of metabolic reactions in aerobic organisms.
source: Glutathione (GSH) is the most abundant antioxidant capable of providing reducing equivalents and it also serves as a versatile nucleophilic cofactor in a wide spectrum of metabolic reactions in aerobic organisms (Kosower and Kosower, 1978; Meister, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Extracellular levels of GSH are normally three orders of magnitude lower than intracellular GSH concentrations.
source: While some cells are capable of employing extracellular GSH, the utilization of extracellular GSH plays a minor role in regulating GSH homeostasis, since the extracellular levels of GSH are normally three orders of magnitude lower than intracellular GSH concentrations, which are usually in the millimolar range (Kosower and Kosower, 1978; Meister, 1982; Perrone et al., 2005; Hwang et al., 1992; Ganguly et al., 2003; Bennett et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2011; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Intracellular GSH concentrations are usually in the millimolar range.
source: While some cells are capable of employing extracellular GSH, the utilization of extracellular GSH plays a minor role in regulating GSH homeostasis, since the extracellular levels of GSH are normally three orders of magnitude lower than intracellular GSH concentrations, which are usually in the millimolar range (Kosower and Kosower, 1978; Meister, 1982; Perrone et al., 2005; Hwang et al., 1992; Ganguly et al., 2003; Bennett et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2011; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Cellular GSH content is largely determined by intracellular production through de novo synthesis and regeneration from GSSG.
source: Hence, cellular GSH content is largely determined by intracellular production through de novo synthesis, a process mediated by two ATP-dependent ligases, glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and glutathione synthase (GS), as well as through regeneration of GSH from GSSG, a process catalyzed by glutathione disulfide reductase (GSR) (Meister, 1982; Lu, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: De novo GSH synthesis is mediated by two ATP-dependent ligases, glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and glutathione synthase (GS).
source: Hence, cellular GSH content is largely determined by intracellular production through de novo synthesis, a process mediated by two ATP-dependent ligases, glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and glutathione synthase (GS), as well as through regeneration of GSH from GSSG, a process catalyzed by glutathione disulfide reductase (GSR) (Meister, 1982; Lu, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Regeneration of GSH from GSSG is catalyzed by glutathione disulfide reductase (GSR).
source: Hence, cellular GSH content is largely determined by intracellular production through de novo synthesis, a process mediated by two ATP-dependent ligases, glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and glutathione synthase (GS), as well as through regeneration of GSH from GSSG, a process catalyzed by glutathione disulfide reductase (GSR) (Meister, 1982; Lu, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GCL is a heterodimer of a catalytic subunit (GCLC) and a modifier subunit (GCLM).
source: In the process of de novo synthesis, GCL, a heterodimer of a catalytic subunit (GCLC) and a modifier subunit (GCLM), catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step to form the dipeptide γ-glutamylcysteine (γ-GC) from cysteine and glutamate (Franklin et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GCL catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step to form the dipeptide γ-glutamylcysteine (γ-GC) from cysteine and glutamate.
source: In the process of de novo synthesis, GCL, a heterodimer of a catalytic subunit (GCLC) and a modifier subunit (GCLM), catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step to form the dipeptide γ-glutamylcysteine (γ-GC) from cysteine and glutamate (Franklin et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GS catalyzes the formation of GSH by ligating γ-GC with glycine.
source: After the initial step, GS catalyzes the formation of GSH by ligating γ-GC with glycine.
evidence: This statement describes a well-established biochemical reaction.

claim: GSH synthesis is determined by the availability of its constituent amino acids, cysteine, glycine and glutamate.
source: As such, GSH synthesis is determined by the availability of its constituent amino acids, cysteine, glycine and glutamate, which intersects with glucose and glutamine metabolic pathways and reflects the overall metabolic status in the cell.
evidence: This statement is based on biochemical knowledge and the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Glutamine catabolism may coordinate with de novo GSH synthesis by promoting cysteine uptake and providing glutamate.
source: In particular, glutamine catabolism may coordinate with de novo GSH synthesis by promoting cysteine uptake and providing glutamate, an immediate product of glutamine after deamination (Altman et al., 2016; Hensley et al., 2013; Gorrini et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Activation of T cells leads to a significant enhancement of aerobic glycolysis.
source: We and others have shown that activation of T cells leads to a significant enhancement of aerobic glycolysis but a suppression of mitochondria-dependent fatty acid oxidation (FAO) (Wang et al., 2011; Frauwirth et al., 2002; Jacobs et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the authors' previous work and other literature.

claim: Activation of T cells leads to a suppression of mitochondria-dependent fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
source: We and others have shown that activation of T cells leads to a significant enhancement of aerobic glycolysis but a suppression of mitochondria-dependent fatty acid oxidation (FAO) (Wang et al., 2011; Frauwirth et al., 2002; Jacobs et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the authors' previous work and other literature.

claim: FAO fuels and drives induced CD4+ regulatory T (Treg) cell differentiation.
source: Following the initial growth stage of T cell activation, FAO fuels and drives induced CD4+ regulatory T (Treg) cell differentiation (Shi et al., 2011; Michalek et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A persistent glycolytic program is engaged throughout the differentiation of CD4+T helper (TH) cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T (CTL) cells.
source: In contrast, a persistent glycolytic program is engaged not only during the initial growth phase of T cell activation but also throughout the differentiation of other CD4+T helper (TH) cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T (CTL) cells (Shi et al., 2011; Michalek et al., 2011; Finlay et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Oxygen consumption is dramatically elevated in active T cells.
source: However, oxygen consumption is also dramatically elevated in active T cells since heightened glutamine catabolism via mitochondria-dependent oxidation following T cell activation fuels oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) by providing α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), an anaplerotic substrate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle) (Wang et al., 2011; Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the authors' previous work and other literature.

claim: Heightened glutamine catabolism following T cell activation fuels oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) by providing α-ketoglutarate (α-KG).
source: However, oxygen consumption is also dramatically elevated in active T cells since heightened glutamine catabolism via mitochondria-dependent oxidation following T cell activation fuels oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) by providing α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), an anaplerotic substrate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle) (Wang et al., 2011; Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the authors' previous work and other literature.

claim: OXPHOS in mitochondria generates ATP through the electron transport chain (ETC) and produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) as byproducts.
source: OXPHOS in mitochondria generates ATP through the electron transport chain (ETC) and also produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) as byproducts, rendering mitochondria a major source of intracellular ROS.
evidence: This statement is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Mitochondria are a major source of intracellular ROS.
source: OXPHOS in mitochondria generates ATP through the electron transport chain (ETC) and also produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) as byproducts, rendering mitochondria a major source of intracellular ROS.
evidence: This statement is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Superoxide anion (O2•−) is the 'primary' ROS derived from mitochondrial ETC.
source: Superoxide anion (O2•−), the 'primary' ROS derived from mitochondrial ETC, is converted to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by spontaneous and enzymatic processes, whereupon H2O2 freely diffuses into cytosol and functions as a redox signaling molecule to elicit a diverse array of cellular responses, the spectrum of which depends on the level of ROS (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012; Murphy, 2009; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Superoxide anion is converted to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by spontaneous and enzymatic processes.
source: Superoxide anion (O2•−), the 'primary' ROS derived from mitochondrial ETC, is converted to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by spontaneous and enzymatic processes, whereupon H2O2 freely diffuses into cytosol and functions as a redox signaling molecule to elicit a diverse array of cellular responses, the spectrum of which depends on the level of ROS (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012; Murphy, 2009; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: H2O2 freely diffuses into cytosol and functions as a redox signaling molecule.
source: Superoxide anion (O2•−), the 'primary' ROS derived from mitochondrial ETC, is converted to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by spontaneous and enzymatic processes, whereupon H2O2 freely diffuses into cytosol and functions as a redox signaling molecule to elicit a diverse array of cellular responses, the spectrum of which depends on the level of ROS (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012; Murphy, 2009; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Physiological levels of intracellular ROS are required for driving essential signaling events to support T cell-mediated immune responses.
source: A fine-tuned balance between ROS generation and antioxidant capacity ensures physiological levels of intracellular ROS, which are required for driving essential signaling events to support T cell-mediated immune responses (Weinberg et al., 2015; Murphy and Siegel, 2013; Kamiński et al., 2013; Simeoni et al., 2016; Rashida Gnanaprakasam et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Oxidative stress dampens essential cellular processes and functions of T cells.
source: Accordingly, oxidative stress, occurring when ROS generation exceeds the capacity of antioxidants, dampens essential cellular processes and functions of T cells.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge and logical inference.

claim: ROS production is induced following T cell activation and is required for driving T cell activation and proliferation.
source: Accumulating evidence has shown that ROS production is induced following T cell activation and is required for driving T cell activation and proliferation (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: TH17 cells are more sensitive to the damaging effects of ROS than are Treg cells.
source: Also, TH17 cells are more sensitive to the damaging effects of ROS than are Treg cells (Gerriets et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: GSH biosynthesis plays a critical role in maintaining ROS homeostasis and regulating Myc-dependent T cell metabolic reprogramming during T cell activation.
source: A recent study demonstrated a critical role for GSH biosynthesis in fine-tuning this process by maintaining ROS hemostasis and regulating Myc-dependent T cell metabolic reprogramming during T cell activation (Mak et al., 2017; Klein Geltink et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: T cell activation is associated with enhanced GSH production.
source: T cell activation is associated with enhanced GSH and ROS production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012; Mak et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to literature.

claim: T cell activation is associated with enhanced ROS production.
source: T cell activation is associated with enhanced GSH and ROS production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012; Mak et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citations to literature.

claim: mRNAs encoding GSH metabolic enzymes are upregulated in T cells following activation in a time-dependent manner.
source: Real time quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis revealed a time-dependent up-regulation of mRNAs encoding these metabolic enzymes in T cells following activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gclm deficiency results in reduced intracellular GSH content in activated T cells.
source: Deficiency in GCLC (the catalytic subunit) and, to a lesser extent, deficiency in GCLM (modifier subunit) resulted in reduced intracellular content of GSH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in reduced intracellular GSH content in activated T cells.
source: Deficiency in GCLC (the catalytic subunit) and, to a lesser extent, deficiency in GCLM (modifier subunit) resulted in reduced intracellular content of GSH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gclm deficiency results in increased ROS in activated T cells.
source: Consistent with this, we observed increased ROS in Gclc- and to a lesser extent in Gclm-deficient T cells as compared to WT T cells. (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in increased ROS in activated T cells.
source: Consistent with this, we observed increased ROS in Gclc- and to a lesser extent in Gclm-deficient T cells as compared to WT T cells. (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WT and Gsr-deficient T cells display comparable GSH levels.
source: However, WT and Gsr-deficient T cells displayed comparable GSH and ROS levels (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WT and Gsr-deficient T cells display comparable ROS levels.
source: However, WT and Gsr-deficient T cells displayed comparable GSH and ROS levels (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: De novo synthesis of GSH plays an indispensable role in producing GSH and maintaining redox homeostasis during T cell activation.
source: These results suggested that de novo synthesis of GSH by the metabolic pathway plays an indispensable role in producing GSH and maintaining redox homeostasis during T cell activation.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the experimental data comparing Gclc/Gclm and Gsr knockout mice.

claim: Gclm KO, T cell-Gclc KO and Gsr KO mice contain comparable numbers and distribution of thymocytes and peripheral CD4+ and CD8+ T cells relative to control mice.
source: Gclm KO, T cell-Gclc KO and Gsr KO mice contained comparable numbers and distribution of thymocytes and peripheral CD4+ and CD8+ T cells relative to control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C and D), indicating a largely undisturbed T cell development and distribution after double positive stage in the absence of GSH recycling pathway or the de novo synthesis pathway.
evidence: This statement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: T cell development and distribution after double positive stage is largely undisturbed in the absence of GSH recycling pathway or the de novo synthesis pathway.
source: Gclm KO, T cell-Gclc KO and Gsr KO mice contained comparable numbers and distribution of thymocytes and peripheral CD4+ and CD8+ T cells relative to control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C and D), indicating a largely undisturbed T cell development and distribution after double positive stage in the absence of GSH recycling pathway or the de novo synthesis pathway.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gclc deficiency suppresses T cell activation and proliferation.
source: A recent study has showed that Gclc deficiency suppressed T cell activation and proliferation, demonstrating a critical role of GCLC in regulating T cell activation (Mak et al., 2017; Klein Geltink et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in an impairment of cell viability in activated T cells.
source: While both Gclc and Gclm deficiency caused a reduction of GSH and induction of ROS, albeit to different degrees (Figure 1B and C), Gclc but not Gclm deficiency resulted in an impairment of cell viability, appearance of the activation marker CD25, and activation-induced cell proliferation (Figure 2A, B, D, E and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in an impairment of CD25 expression in activated T cells.
source: While both Gclc and Gclm deficiency caused a reduction of GSH and induction of ROS, albeit to different degrees (Figure 1B and C), Gclc but not Gclm deficiency resulted in an impairment of cell viability, appearance of the activation marker CD25, and activation-induced cell proliferation (Figure 2A, B, D, E and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by CD25 expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in an impairment of activation-induced cell proliferation.
source: While both Gclc and Gclm deficiency caused a reduction of GSH and induction of ROS, albeit to different degrees (Figure 1B and C), Gclc but not Gclm deficiency resulted in an impairment of cell viability, appearance of the activation marker CD25, and activation-induced cell proliferation (Figure 2A, B, D, E and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Gclm deficiency does not impair cell viability in activated T cells.
source: While both Gclc and Gclm deficiency caused a reduction of GSH and induction of ROS, albeit to different degrees (Figure 1B and C), Gclc but not Gclm deficiency resulted in an impairment of cell viability, appearance of the activation marker CD25, and activation-induced cell proliferation (Figure 2A, B, D, E and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Gclm deficiency does not impair CD25 expression in activated T cells.
source: While both Gclc and Gclm deficiency caused a reduction of GSH and induction of ROS, albeit to different degrees (Figure 1B and C), Gclc but not Gclm deficiency resulted in an impairment of cell viability, appearance of the activation marker CD25, and activation-induced cell proliferation (Figure 2A, B, D, E and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by CD25 expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Gclm deficiency does not impair activation-induced cell proliferation.
source: While both Gclc and Gclm deficiency caused a reduction of GSH and induction of ROS, albeit to different degrees (Figure 1B and C), Gclc but not Gclm deficiency resulted in an impairment of cell viability, appearance of the activation marker CD25, and activation-induced cell proliferation (Figure 2A, B, D, E and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GSH depletion causes inactivation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and leads to ferroptosis.
source: Previous studies have shown that GSH depletion caused inactivation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), and consequentially led to iron-dependent accumulation of lipid peroxidation and a form of cell necrosis referred as ferroptosis (Stockwell et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Reduced cell viability in Gclc-deficient T cells is likely due to ferroptosis in the context of GSH depletion.
source: Our data suggested that a moderate reduced cell viability in Gclc-deficient T cells is likely due to ferroptosis in the context of GSH depletion (Figure 2G).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the cell viability data and knowledge about ferroptosis.

claim: Active T cells can tolerate and cope with a moderate depletion of GSH and induction of ROS caused by Gclm deficiency.
source: Our results suggested that a severe depletion of GSH and induction of ROS caused by Gclc deficiency significantly impaired T cell activation and proliferation, however, active T cell could tolerate and cope with a moderate depletion of GSH and induction of ROS caused by Gclm deficiency.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the differential effects of Gclc and Gclm deficiency on T cell activation.

claim: Gsr deficiency does not impair T cell viability.
source: Consistent with its dispensable role in GSH production in active T cells (Figure 1B and C), Gsr deficiency did not lead to any impairment of T cell viability, activation marker CD25 and proliferation (Figures 2C, F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Gsr deficiency does not impair CD25 expression in activated T cells.
source: Consistent with its dispensable role in GSH production in active T cells (Figure 1B and C), Gsr deficiency did not lead to any impairment of T cell viability, activation marker CD25 and proliferation (Figures 2C, F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by CD25 expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Gsr deficiency does not impair T cell proliferation.
source: Consistent with its dispensable role in GSH production in active T cells (Figure 1B and C), Gsr deficiency did not lead to any impairment of T cell viability, activation marker CD25 and proliferation (Figures 2C, F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: None of the genetic deficiencies (Gclc, Gclm, or Gsr) compromise the early activation marker CD69.
source: Notably, none of the above genetic deficiencies compromised the early activation marker CD69 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by CD69 expression data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: GSH recycling pathway is dispensable in regulating T cell activation and proliferation.
source: Our results suggest that GSH recycling pathway is dispensable in regulating T cell activation and proliferation.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the Gsr knockout data.

claim: Gclm KO cells exhibit reduced IL-17+ cells compared to WT cells under TH17 differentiation conditions.
source: As compared to control WT cells, Gclm KO cells exhibited reduced IL-17+ and increased Foxp3+ cells (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gclm KO cells exhibit increased Foxp3+ cells compared to WT cells under iTreg differentiation conditions.
source: As compared to control WT cells, Gclm KO cells exhibited reduced IL-17+ and increased Foxp3+ cells (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: WT and Gclm KO CD4+ T cells display a similar degree of proliferation.
source: Given that a similar degree of proliferation was observed between WT and Gclm KO CD4+ T cells (Figure 3A and D), deregulation of cell differentiation in Gclm KO was largely independent of cell expansion.
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: Deregulation of cell differentiation in Gclm KO is largely independent of cell expansion.
source: Given that a similar degree of proliferation was observed between WT and Gclm KO CD4+ T cells (Figure 3A and D), deregulation of cell differentiation in Gclm KO was largely independent of cell expansion.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the proliferation and differentiation data.

claim: Acute deletion of Gclc bypasses its requirement for cell proliferation.
source: As compared with WT cells, acute deletion of Gclc bypassed its required for cell proliferation, as revealed by a comparable CFSE dilution (Figure 3B and E), but nevertheless resulted in a reduction in the generation of IL-17+ T cells and an induction in the generation of Foxp3+ cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: Acute deletion of Gclc results in a reduction in the generation of IL-17+ T cells.
source: As compared with WT cells, acute deletion of Gclc bypassed its required for cell proliferation, as revealed by a comparable CFSE dilution (Figure 3B and E), but nevertheless resulted in a reduction in the generation of IL-17+ T cells and an induction in the generation of Foxp3+ cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Acute deletion of Gclc results in an induction in the generation of Foxp3+ cells.
source: As compared with WT cells, acute deletion of Gclc bypassed its required for cell proliferation, as revealed by a comparable CFSE dilution (Figure 3B and E), but nevertheless resulted in a reduction in the generation of IL-17+ T cells and an induction in the generation of Foxp3+ cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Gsr KO and WT CD4+ T cells display a similar degree of TH17 differentiation.
source: In contrast to the effects of ablation of Gclm and Gclc, Gsr KO and WT CD4+ T cells displayed a similar degree of TH17 and iTreg differentiation, indicating a dispensable role for recycling GSSG in regulating T cell differentiation (Figure 3C and F).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gsr KO and WT CD4+ T cells display a similar degree of iTreg differentiation.
source: In contrast to the effects of ablation of Gclm and Gclc, Gsr KO and WT CD4+ T cells displayed a similar degree of TH17 and iTreg differentiation, indicating a dispensable role for recycling GSSG in regulating T cell differentiation (Figure 3C and F).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Recycling GSSG plays a dispensable role in regulating T cell differentiation.
source: In contrast to the effects of ablation of Gclm and Gclc, Gsr KO and WT CD4+ T cells displayed a similar degree of TH17 and iTreg differentiation, indicating a dispensable role for recycling GSSG in regulating T cell differentiation (Figure 3C and F).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the Gsr knockout data.

claim: NAC restores TH17 cell differentiation in Gclc-/- T cells.
source: The addition of N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC), a reagent often used to scavenge ROS, restored TH17 cell differentiation in Gclc-/- T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NAC scavenges ROS independently of GSH synthesis.
source: Consistent with these, our result suggests that NAC scavenges ROS independently of GSH synthesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D) and therefore restores TH17 cell differentiation in Gclc-/- T cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS and GSH measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Genetic ablation of GCLM confers protection against EAE disease progression.
source: Genetic ablation of GCLM or GCLC conferred a protection against disease progression (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This statement is supported by EAE scoring data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Genetic ablation of GCLC confers protection against EAE disease progression.
source: Genetic ablation of GCLM or GCLC conferred a protection against disease progression (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This statement is supported by EAE scoring data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: De novo synthesis of GSH is required for TH17 development in vitro.
source: Collectively, our studies suggested that de novo synthesis of GSH is required for TH17 development in vitro and TH17-driven CNS inflammation in vivo.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the in vitro differentiation experiments.

claim: De novo synthesis of GSH is required for TH17-driven CNS inflammation in vivo.
source: Collectively, our studies suggested that de novo synthesis of GSH is required for TH17 development in vitro and TH17-driven CNS inflammation in vivo.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the EAE experiments.

claim: TH17 cells display a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells at day 3.
source: TH17 cells displayed a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells. In contrast, the level of ROS was lower in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TH17 cells display a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells at day 5.
source: TH17 cells displayed a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells. In contrast, the level of ROS was lower in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of ROS is lower in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells at day 3.
source: TH17 cells displayed a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells. In contrast, the level of ROS was lower in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The level of ROS is lower in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells at day 5.
source: TH17 cells displayed a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells. In contrast, the level of ROS was lower in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TH17 cells display a higher level of intracellular GSH than iTreg cells as measured by mass spectrometry.
source: In addition, TH17 cells displayed a higher level of intracellular GSH and GSSG than iTreg cells, as revealed by mass spectrometry (Figure 4C).
evidence: This statement is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TH17 cells display a higher level of intracellular GSSG than iTreg cells as measured by mass spectrometry.
source: In addition, TH17 cells displayed a higher level of intracellular GSH and GSSG than iTreg cells, as revealed by mass spectrometry (Figure 4C).
evidence: This statement is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NRF2 controls the expression of genes involved in producing, regenerating, and utilizing GSH.
source: A key cellular mechanism in defending against oxidative stress is through activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), which controls the expression of genes involved in producing, regenerating, and utilizing GSH. NRF2 also controls other antioxidant pathways that regulate thioredoxin (TXN), NADPH generation and iron sequestration (Jaramillo and Zhang, 2013; Sporn and Liby, 2012; Ma, 2013; Motohashi and Yamamoto, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: NRF2 controls other antioxidant pathways that regulate thioredoxin (TXN), NADPH generation and iron sequestration.
source: A key cellular mechanism in defending against oxidative stress is through activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), which controls the expression of genes involved in producing, regenerating, and utilizing GSH. NRF2 also controls other antioxidant pathways that regulate thioredoxin (TXN), NADPH generation and iron sequestration (Jaramillo and Zhang, 2013; Sporn and Liby, 2012; Ma, 2013; Motohashi and Yamamoto, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: NRF2 and its target genes are highly upregulated in TH17 cells compared to iTreg cells.
source: Also, qPCR analyses revealed marked upregulation of genes encoding various molecules involved in glutamine catabolism and GSH metabolism in TH17 compared to iTreg cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TH17 cells preferentially maintain a low degree of oxidative stress by engaging the NRF2 signaling pathway.
source: Consistent with increased levels of GSH and decreased levels of ROS in TH17 cells, qPCR analysis revealed a time-dependent up-regulation of mRNAs encoding NRF2 and its target genes, including glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), TXN, thioredoxin reductase 1 (Txnrd1), CD44, heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (Nqo1) and glutathione synthetase (Gss) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). These results suggested that TH17 cells preferentially maintain a low degree of oxidative stress by a tight regulation of GSH synthesis and ROS homeostasis.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the qPCR data and GSH/ROS measurements.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in reduced intracellular GSH content during TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Deficiency in Gclc and, to a lesser extent, deficiency in Gclm resulted in reduced intracellular content of GSH (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gclm deficiency results in reduced intracellular GSH content during TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Deficiency in Gclc and, to a lesser extent, deficiency in Gclm resulted in reduced intracellular content of GSH (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gclc deficiency results in increased ROS during TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Consistent with this, we observed increased ROS in Gclc- and Gclm-deficient T cells as compared to WT T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Gclm deficiency results in increased ROS during TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Consistent with this, we observed increased ROS in Gclc- and Gclm-deficient T cells as compared to WT T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: WT and Gsr-deficient T cells display comparable GSH levels during TH17 differentiation.
source: By contrast, WT and Gsr-deficient T cells displayed comparable GSH sand ROS levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: WT and Gsr-deficient T cells display comparable ROS levels during TH17 differentiation.
source: By contrast, WT and Gsr-deficient T cells displayed comparable GSH sand ROS levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The recycling pathway is dispensable in producing GSH and maintaining redox homeostasis during TH17 differentiation.
source: These results indicated that the preferential requirement for de novo synthesis of GSH during the initial T cell activation stage is extended to the later T cell differentiation stage. However, the recycling pathway is dispensable in producing GSH and maintaining redox homeostasis during TH17 differentiation.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the Gsr knockout data during TH17 differentiation.

claim: Addition of 1 μM H2O2 does not impact cell proliferation.
source: Addition of 1 μM H2O2 did not impact cell proliferation but reciprocally reduced TH17 and enhanced iTreg cell differentiation (Figure 5A and B), indicating that its effect on differentiation was largely independent of expansion.
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of 1 μM H2O2 reciprocally reduces TH17 and enhances iTreg cell differentiation.
source: Addition of 1 μM H2O2 did not impact cell proliferation but reciprocally reduced TH17 and enhanced iTreg cell differentiation (Figure 5A and B), indicating that its effect on differentiation was largely independent of expansion.
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of H2O2 on T cell differentiation is largely independent of cell expansion.
source: Addition of 1 μM H2O2 did not impact cell proliferation but reciprocally reduced TH17 and enhanced iTreg cell differentiation (Figure 5A and B), indicating that its effect on differentiation was largely independent of expansion.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the proliferation and differentiation data.

claim: DMF treatment displays a dosage-dependent suppression of TH17 cell differentiation.
source: DMF treatment displayed a dosage-dependent suppression of TH17 cell differentiation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At lower doses (20–50 μM), DMF displays minimal inhibitory effects on cell proliferation.
source: Although the addition of 75 μM DMF inhibited T cell proliferation, at the lower dose of DMF used in this study (20–50 μM), we observed minimal inhibitory effects of DMF on cell proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that DMF-mediated suppression on TH17 differentiation was largely independent of cell proliferation.
evidence: This statement is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DMF-mediated suppression on TH17 differentiation is largely independent of cell proliferation.
source: Although the addition of 75 μM DMF inhibited T cell proliferation, at the lower dose of DMF used in this study (20–50 μM), we observed minimal inhibitory effects of DMF on cell proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that DMF-mediated suppression on TH17 differentiation was largely independent of cell proliferation.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the proliferation and differentiation data.

claim: DMF treatments induce ROS production in TH17 cells.
source: Moreover, DMF treatments induced ROS production in TH17 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NAC restores TH17 cell differentiation in the presence of DMF.
source: Consistent with the idea that DMF suppresses TH17 cell differentiation through the induction of oxidative stress, the addition of N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) restored TH17 cell differentiation in the presence of DMF (Figure 5E).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DMF suppresses TH17 cell differentiation through the induction of oxidative stress.
source: Consistent with the idea that DMF suppresses TH17 cell differentiation through the induction of oxidative stress, the addition of N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) restored TH17 cell differentiation in the presence of DMF (Figure 5E).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the NAC rescue experiment.

claim: DMF at doses of 5 and 20 μM fails to affect iTreg cell differentiation in vitro.
source: However, the doses of DMF (5 and 20 μM) that could suppress TH17 differentiation failed to affect iTreg cell differentiation in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DMF may partially exert its immunomodulatory action through the augmentation of oxidative stress and suppressing TH17 differentiation.
source: As such, our data suggested that DMF may partially exert its immunomodulatory action through the augmentation of oxidative stress and suppressing TH17 differentiation.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the DMF experiments.

claim: The 13C5 isotopologues of glutamate represent a significant fraction of the total glutamate pool in TH17 cells.
source: The 13C5 isotopologues (generated via a direct Glutamine to Glutmate conversion) represented a significant fraction of the total glutamate and GSH pool in both TH17 and iTreg cells, however, the absolute quantity of 13C5-glutamate and 13C5-GSH is higher in TH17 cells than in iTreg cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The 13C5 isotopologues of GSH represent a significant fraction of the total GSH pool in TH17 cells.
source: The 13C5 isotopologues (generated via a direct Glutamine to Glutmate conversion) represented a significant fraction of the total glutamate and GSH pool in both TH17 and iTreg cells, however, the absolute quantity of 13C5-glutamate and 13C5-GSH is higher in TH17 cells than in iTreg cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The absolute quantity of 13C5-glutamate is higher in TH17 cells than in iTreg cells.
source: The 13C5 isotopologues (generated via a direct Glutamine to Glutmate conversion) represented a significant fraction of the total glutamate and GSH pool in both TH17 and iTreg cells, however, the absolute quantity of 13C5-glutamate and 13C5-GSH is higher in TH17 cells than in iTreg cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The absolute quantity of 13C5-GSH is higher in TH17 cells than in iTreg cells.
source: The 13C5 isotopologues (generated via a direct Glutamine to Glutmate conversion) represented a significant fraction of the total glutamate and GSH pool in both TH17 and iTreg cells, however, the absolute quantity of 13C5-glutamate and 13C5-GSH is higher in TH17 cells than in iTreg cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TH17 cells can uptake more glutamine and/or produce more glutamate for GSH synthesis than iTreg cells.
source: These results suggested that TH17 cells could uptake more glutamine and/or produce more glutamate for GSH synthesis than iTreg cells.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the isotope tracing data.

claim: Glutamine starvation reduces GSH content in a time-dependent manner in TH17 cells.
source: In accord with this data, glutamine starvation reduced GSH content in a time-dependent manner in TH17 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by GSH measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TH17 cells display higher glutamine oxidation activity than iTreg cells.
source: TH17 cells displayed higher glutamine oxidation activity, indicated by 14CO2 release from [U-14C]-glutamine, than did iTreg cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This statement is supported by radiochemical assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mitochondria-dependent pyruvate oxidation through the TCA cycle is comparable between TH17 and iTreg cells.
source: However, mitochondria-dependent pyruvate oxidation through the TCA cycle, indicated by 14CO2 release from [2-14C]-pyruvate, was comparable between the two functional subsets (Figure 6C).
evidence: This statement is supported by radiochemical assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Genes encoding molecules involved in glutamine catabolism are upregulated in TH17 compared to iTreg cells.
source: Also, qPCR analyses revealed marked upregulation of genes encoding various molecules involved in glutamine catabolism and GSH metabolism in TH17 compared to iTreg cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genes encoding molecules involved in GSH metabolism are upregulated in TH17 compared to iTreg cells.
source: Also, qPCR analyses revealed marked upregulation of genes encoding various molecules involved in glutamine catabolism and GSH metabolism in TH17 compared to iTreg cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Deprivation of glutamine significantly suppresses TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Consistent with this, deprivation of glutamine significantly suppressed TH17 but moderately enhanced iTreg cell differentiation (Figure 6D), while both TH17 and iTreg differentiation required glucose (Figure 6E).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Deprivation of glutamine moderately enhances iTreg cell differentiation.
source: Consistent with this, deprivation of glutamine significantly suppressed TH17 but moderately enhanced iTreg cell differentiation (Figure 6D), while both TH17 and iTreg differentiation required glucose (Figure 6E).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both TH17 and iTreg differentiation require glucose.
source: Consistent with this, deprivation of glutamine significantly suppressed TH17 but moderately enhanced iTreg cell differentiation (Figure 6D), while both TH17 and iTreg differentiation required glucose (Figure 6E).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: BPTES slightly enhances IL-17 expression.
source: Two Gls1 specific inhibitors, bis-2-(5-phenylacetamido-1,2,4-thiadiazol-2-yl) ethyl sulfide (BPTES) and CB-839 (Wang et al., 2010; Le et al., 2012), slightly enhanced IL-17 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CB-839 slightly enhances IL-17 expression.
source: Two Gls1 specific inhibitors, bis-2-(5-phenylacetamido-1,2,4-thiadiazol-2-yl) ethyl sulfide (BPTES) and CB-839 (Wang et al., 2010; Le et al., 2012), slightly enhanced IL-17 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DON skews T cells away from TH17 toward iTreg differentiation.
source: However, 6-diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON), an analog of glutamine with broad inhibitory effects glutamine utilizing enzymes (Pinkus, 1977; Shapiro et al., 1979), skewed away T cells from TH17 toward iTreg differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DON but not BPTES and CB-839 significantly enhances ROS production under TH17-polarizing condition.
source: In addition, DON but not BPTES and CB-839 significantly enhanced ROS production under TH17-polarizing condition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Addition of hypoxanthine and thymidine (HT) partially rescues TH17 differentiation in glutamine-free condition.
source: In line with this report, addition of either hypoxanthine and thymidine (HT) or α-KG was able to partially rescue TH17 differentiation in glutamine-free condition without impacting ROS level (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Addition of α-KG partially rescues TH17 differentiation in glutamine-free condition.
source: In line with this report, addition of either hypoxanthine and thymidine (HT) or α-KG was able to partially rescue TH17 differentiation in glutamine-free condition without impacting ROS level (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Addition of HT or α-KG does not impact ROS level in glutamine-free condition.
source: In line with this report, addition of either hypoxanthine and thymidine (HT) or α-KG was able to partially rescue TH17 differentiation in glutamine-free condition without impacting ROS level (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: NAC treatment alone is incapable of rescuing TH17 differentiation in the absence of glutamine.
source: While NAC treatment is sufficient to suppress ROS production, it was incapable of rescuing TH17 differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The combination of HT and NAC leads to more differentiated TH17 cells compared to HT treatment alone in the absence of glutamine.
source: However, the combination of HT and NAC led to more differentiated TH17 cells and lower level of ROS comparing to HT treatment alone in the absence of glutamine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Glutamine catabolism directs the lineage choices between TH17 and iTreg cells through supporting T cell proliferation by providing biosynthetic precursors.
source: Taken together, our studies suggest that glutamine catabolism directs the lineage choices between TH17 and iTreg cells through supporting T cell proliferation by providing biosynthetic precursors.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the glutamine deprivation and rescue experiments.

claim: Glutamine-derived glutamate provides a key substrate for the de novo synthesis of GSH and modulates ROS signaling.
source: In addition, glutamine-derived glutamate provides a key substrate for the de novo synthesis of GSH, modulates ROS signaling, and may also impact T cell differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the isotope tracing and functional experiments.

claim: Glucose plays an indispensable role in driving TH17 and iTreg cell differentiation.
source: Here, we found that glucose plays an indispensable role in driving TH17 and iTreg cell differentiation, while glutamine is only required for TH17 cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by glucose deprivation experiments.

claim: Glutamine is only required for TH17 cell differentiation.
source: Here, we found that glucose plays an indispensable role in driving TH17 and iTreg cell differentiation, while glutamine is only required for TH17 cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by glutamine deprivation experiments.

claim: Glutamine catabolism is coupled with de novo GSH synthesis and is preferentially elevated during TH17 but not iTreg cell differentiation.
source: Glutamine catabolism is coupled with de novo GSH synthesis and is preferentially elevated during TH17 but not iTreg cell differentiation, suggesting that different T cell lineages 'wire' metabolism differently to support their development and function.
evidence: This statement is supported by isotope tracing and metabolic activity measurements.

claim: Different T cell lineages 'wire' metabolism differently to support their development and function.
source: Glutamine catabolism is coupled with de novo GSH synthesis and is preferentially elevated during TH17 but not iTreg cell differentiation, suggesting that different T cell lineages 'wire' metabolism differently to support their development and function.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the differential metabolic requirements of TH17 and iTreg cells.

claim: HIF1α coordinates glycolysis and T cell signaling cascades to regulate the differentiation of TH17 and iTreg cells.
source: Previous studies have suggested that engagement of the transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) coordinates glycolysis and T cell signaling cascades to regulate the differentiation of TH17 and iTreg cells (Shi et al., 2011; Dang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Glycolysis provides ATP and biosynthetic precursors for glycine, fulfilling the needs of de novo synthesis of GSH during T cell differentiation.
source: While the high rate of glutamine catabolism ensures the capacity to supply glutamate, glycolysis provides ATP and biosynthetic precursors for glycine, fulfilling the needs of de novo synthesis of GSH during T cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on metabolic knowledge and the experimental findings.

claim: De novo synthesis of GSH but not recycling from GSSG is required for fine-tuning ROS and directing the differentiation of TH17 and Treg cells.
source: Our results using genetic modulation of metabolic enzymes suggest that de novo synthesis of GSH but not recycling from GSSG is required for fine-tuning ROS and directing the differentiation of TH17 and Treg cells.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the genetic knockout experiments.

claim: Dimethyl fumarate suppresses TH17 differentiation by augmenting intracellular ROS.
source: We further found that dimethyl fumarate, a FDA approved drug (BG-12/Tecfidera) for multiple sclerosis, suppresses TH17 differentiation by augmenting intracellular ROS.
evidence: This statement is supported by DMF treatment experiments showing increased ROS and decreased TH17 differentiation.

claim: ROS are essential metabolic signals that dictate T cell lineage engagement.
source: While previous studies clearly demonstrate that activation-induced metabolic reprogramming is required for driving T cell growth and proliferation, our studies shed light on the complex utilization of the glutamine catabolic pathway and implicate ROS as essential metabolic signals that dictate T cell lineage engagement.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: TCR engagement induces a rapid generation of mitochondrial ROS from OXPHOS and cytoplasmic ROS from NADPH oxidases (NOXs).
source: T cell receptor (TCR) engagement induces a rapid generation of mitochondrial ROS from OXPHOS and cytoplasmic ROS from NADPH oxidases (NOXs), a family of plasma membrane associated oxidases (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: T cells with reduced production of mitochondrial ROS display impaired production of interleukin 2 (IL-2) and antigen-specific proliferation.
source: T cells with reduced production of mitochondrial ROS display impaired production of interleukin 2 (IL-2) and antigen-specific proliferation, indicating an essential signaling role for mitochondrial ROS in driving optimal TCR signaling (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Mitochondrial ROS plays an essential signaling role in driving optimal TCR signaling.
source: T cells with reduced production of mitochondrial ROS display impaired production of interleukin 2 (IL-2) and antigen-specific proliferation, indicating an essential signaling role for mitochondrial ROS in driving optimal TCR signaling (Sena et al., 2013; Kamiński et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: T cells with low levels of ROS due to NOX deficiency are skewed toward a TH17 phenotype.
source: T cells with low levels of ROS due to NOX deficiency are skewed toward a TH17 phenotype (Jackson et al., 2004; Purushothaman and Sarin, 2009; Padgett and Tse, 2016; Tse et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: De novo synthesis of GSH is essential for fine-tuning ROS levels in T cells.
source: Our studies suggest that de novo synthesis of GSH is essential for fine-tuning ROS levels in T cells and also indicate the differential requirements for the level of ROS in driving T cell lineage engagement toward TH17 or iTreg cells.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the genetic knockout experiments.

claim: There are differential requirements for the level of ROS in driving T cell lineage engagement toward TH17 or iTreg cells.
source: Our studies suggest that de novo synthesis of GSH is essential for fine-tuning ROS levels in T cells and also indicate the differential requirements for the level of ROS in driving T cell lineage engagement toward TH17 or iTreg cells.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the experimental findings showing differential ROS levels in TH17 and iTreg cells.

claim: DMF is a cellular permeable analog of fumarate and the key active ingredient of BG-12/TECFIDERA and FUMADERM.
source: Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a cellular permeable analog of fumarate and the key active ingredient of BG-12/TECFIDERA and FUMADERM, a first-line oral treatment for relapsing multiple sclerosis (CONFIRM Study Investigators et al., 2012; ALLEGRO Study Group et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical trial literature.

claim: BG-12/TECFIDERA is a first-line oral treatment for relapsing multiple sclerosis.
source: Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a cellular permeable analog of fumarate and the key active ingredient of BG-12/TECFIDERA and FUMADERM, a first-line oral treatment for relapsing multiple sclerosis (CONFIRM Study Investigators et al., 2012; ALLEGRO Study Group et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical trial literature.

claim: DMF has been suggested to impact Nrf2 and GPCRs in T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), endothelial cells, and neurons.
source: DMF has been suggested to impact a plethora of cellular and molecular targets, including Nrf2 and GPCRs in T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), endothelial cells, and neurons (Blewett et al., 2016; Schulze-Topphoff et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2012; Linker and Gold, 2013; Duffy et al., 1998; Gill and Kolson, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: DMF can neutralize GSH in vitro.
source: Consistent with the studies showing that DMF can neutralize GSH in vitro (Zheng et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2013), our data indicate that the ability of DMF to augment ROS and suppress TH17 cell differentiation contributes to its therapeutic effect.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The ability of DMF to augment ROS and suppress TH17 cell differentiation contributes to its therapeutic effect.
source: Consistent with the studies showing that DMF can neutralize GSH in vitro (Zheng et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2013), our data indicate that the ability of DMF to augment ROS and suppress TH17 cell differentiation contributes to its therapeutic effect.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the DMF experiments.

claim: NRF2 and its target genes are highly upregulated in TH17 cells.
source: Also, NRF2 and its target genes were highly upregulated in TH17 cells, suggesting that TH17 cells preferentially maintain a low degree of oxidative stress partially by engaging the NRF2 signaling pathway.
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data.

claim: NRF2 controls thioredoxin (TXN) production and consumption through transcriptional regulation of its target genes including thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1).
source: In addition to GSH production and consumption, NRF2 controls thioredoxin (TXN) production and consumption through transcriptional regulation of its target genes including thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about NRF2 function.

claim: GSH and TXN are important anti-oxidation systems and appear functionally redundant in most organisms.
source: Both GSH and TXN are important anti-oxidation systems and appear functionally redundant in most organisms (Couto et al., 2016; Mustacich and Powis, 2000; Lei et al., 2016; Lu and Holmgren, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: There is a dynamic cross-talk between the GSH and TXN systems.
source: However, recent studies implicate the presence of a dynamic cross-talk between these two systems.
evidence: This statement is based on recent literature findings.

claim: Glutaredoxin (GRX)-GSH can reduce oxidized TXN in the absence of thioredoxin reductase.
source: Glutaredoxin (GRX)-GSH can reduce oxidized TXN in the absence of thioredoxin reductase. Conversely, TXN-TXNRD can also function as an alternative system to reduce GSSG to GSH (Du et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2004; Hanschmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: TXN-TXNRD can function as an alternative system to reduce GSSG to GSH.
source: Glutaredoxin (GRX)-GSH can reduce oxidized TXN in the absence of thioredoxin reductase. Conversely, TXN-TXNRD can also function as an alternative system to reduce GSSG to GSH (Du et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2004; Hanschmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The TXN and GSH systems can backup for each other under certain conditions.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the TXN and GSH systems can backup for each other under certain conditions.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the cited literature about cross-talk between the systems.

claim: The inhibition of TXNRD renders cancer cells susceptible to the depletion of GSH.
source: Consistent with the overlapping function of the GSH and TXN system, the inhibition of TXNRD rendered cancer cells susceptible to the depletion of GSH (Mandal et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Thioredoxin reductase may partially compensate for the loss of Gsr by backing up the recycle of GSSG to GSH in T cells.
source: Although our data suggest that the de novo synthesis of GSH is sufficient to maintain ROS homeostasis in the absence of Gsr dependent GSSG-GSH recycling, it is still conceivable that thioredoxin reductase may partially compensate for the loss of Gsr by backing up the recycle of GSSG to GSH in T cells.
evidence: This statement is speculation based on the known functions of the TXN system.

claim: TXN can be secreted by CD4+ T cells and may modulate the expression of T cell surface receptor and proliferation.
source: It has been shown that TXN can be secreted by CD4+ T cells and may modulate the expression of T cell surface receptor and proliferation (Rosen et al., 1995; Wakasugi et al., 1990; Matthias et al., 2002; Tagaya et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The combination of DMF and pharmacological approaches that target TXN system may represent a more effective strategy than DMF alone for treating T cell-mediated inflammation and autoimmune disease.
source: As such, we envision that the combination of DMF and pharmacological approaches that target TXN system may represent a more effective strategy than DMF alone for treating T cell-mediated inflammation and autoimmune disease.
evidence: This statement is speculation based on the experimental findings and knowledge about the TXN system.
